title: Independent personal pronouns

objectives.can: Recognise the independent personal pronouns and their person, gender and number.

explanation.summary: Hebrew has a separate set of personal pronouns: 'I', 'you', 'he', 'she', 'we', 'they'. They are separate words, unlike the pronoun endings you will meet on verbs and nouns. They name the subject of a clause with no verb, and they add emphasis when a verb is present.

sections.heading: The set
body: Each pronoun shows a person (first, second or third), a number (singular or plural) and, except in the first person, a gender. The first person has one form for both genders, which grammarians call 'common'.

The corpus files each pronoun under one headword. The feminine singular הִיא is filed under the headword הוּא, and the longer הֵמָּה under הֵם. You will therefore see two different spellings under one headword, with the same person, gender and number.

sections.heading: Two words for 'I'
body: There are two first person singular pronouns, אֲנִי and the fuller אָנֹכִי. Both are common. Which one a writer chooses is not a difference of person or number, and you should not look for a difference in meaning where the translation does not show one. They sometimes stand side by side in the same chapter, for example in Genesis 15:7 and Exodus 20:2.

sections.heading: Subject of a clause without a verb
body: Hebrew has no present tense of 'to be' in simple statements. A pronoun, a noun or a name can simply be set beside another noun: the clause 'I (am) the LORD' needs no verb. The pronoun is the subject, and the second element says who or what the subject is. The time reference comes from the context, so the same words may be read as 'am', 'is', 'are', 'was' or 'were'.

The third person pronoun often does a further job in such clauses: it joins two nouns, as in a definition or an explanation, and can be translated 'it is' or 'this is'. You will meet it in this way in the Hebrew of Genesis 2:14.

sections.heading: Pronouns beside a verb
body: A Hebrew verb already shows its person, gender and number in its endings. When a separate pronoun is added as well, it usually emphasises the subject, or sets it against someone else: 'you, not someone else'. Compare Genesis 45:8, where the pronoun beside the verb stresses who did the sending.
The pronouns are not used for an object. Pronouns that are objects, or that follow prepositions, are written as endings and are met in later lessons.

sections.heading: Reading the forms
body: Look at the first letters. Second person forms begin with אַת (אַתָּה, אַתְּ, אַתֶּם, אַתֵּן). Third person forms begin with ה (הוּא, הִיא, הֵם, הֵנָּה). First person forms begin with אָנ or אֲנ. In the plural, the masculine forms end in ם and the feminine forms in a נ (הֵנָּה, אַתֵּן).

misunderstandings: הֵנָּה is not only the feminine 'they'. The same spelling is also an adverb meaning 'here' or 'hither', and the corpus tags it so in Genesis 45:8. Check the verse before you decide.
A pronoun beside a verb is not a mistake or a repetition. The verb's own endings already name the subject; the separate pronoun adds emphasis or contrast.
הוּא and הִיא do not mean 'the' or 'that' by themselves. With the article (הַהוּא) they can point to something, 'that', but that is a different use, taught with the demonstratives.
The first person has no feminine form. A woman and a man both say אֲנִי.

deeper.heading: Written forms of the feminine 'she'
body: In the Pentateuch the feminine singular is often spelled הִוא, with a vowel letter that looks like the masculine הוּא, and the vowel point of the later reading tradition shows that it is read hi. The corpus keeps both spellings under one headword. In a few verses the same spelling occurs for the masculine; the context and the verb's gender then decide.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And He said unto him: 'I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: אֲנִי is first person singular, the subject of a clause with no verb: 'I (am) the LORD'. The pronoun does not agree with a gender because the first person has none.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And she called the name of the LORD that spoke unto her, Thou art a God of seeing; for she said: 'Have I even here seen Him that seeth Me?'

examples.analysis: אַתָּה is second person masculine singular, addressed to God. As in the previous example, there is no verb: 'you (are) a God of seeing'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Joseph remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them, and said unto them: 'Ye are spies; to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: אַתֶּם is second person masculine plural, 'you'. Joseph speaks to his brothers. The predicate comes first and the pronoun follows it, so the emphasis falls on 'spies': 'spies you (are)'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the man said: 'The woman whom Thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: הִוא is third person feminine singular and agrees with הָאִשָּׁה, 'the woman'. It stands beside the verb נָתְנָה, which already says 'she gave'. The pronoun points to her, with emphasis: 'she, she gave me'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Jacob said unto them: 'My brethren, whence are ye?' And they said: 'Of Haran are we.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two pronouns in one exchange. אַתֶּם is 'you' (plural), in the question 'where are you from?', with no verb. The answer uses אֲנָחְנוּ, first person plural, 'we (are)'. Both are subjects of clauses without a verb.
